claims.claim: Structurally related aryloxypropanolamine and methoxyphenyl-piperazine analogs have measured oral bioavailability values well above the 20% threshold: urapidil 72–78%, pamatolol 64.9–103.5%, metoprolol 84% in cirrhosis, and propranolol 54–79% in cirrhosis.
L3 oral exposure records show measurable oral AUC and Cmax for related compounds, consistent with meaningful oral absorption; none provides affirmative evidence of F below 20%.

L4 dissolution and solubility records show rapid dissolution for naftopidil, a piperazine aryloxypropanol analog, and aqueous solubility for beta-blocker salts, supporting a favorable absorption component.

L5 Caco-2 records show high apparent permeability for methoxyphenyl-piperazine aryloxypropanol analogs (MF-8 series, Papp 16.4–25.6 × 10^-6 cm/s) and for high-permeability beta-blocker controls; no record demonstrates dominant efflux or intestinal metabolism that would drive F below 20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct experimental absolute oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule itself.
L3 exposure records lack intravenous comparators, so they cannot quantify absolute F.
L5 Caco-2 records are mechanistic permeability/efflux assays, not in vivo F; no query-specific intestinal metabolism or first-pass data are available.
Reference values were obtained under cirrhosis, fed, or modified-release conditions that may not match the query condition.
No exact analog with the same piperazine-acetamide-2,6-dimethylanilide substructure has a measured F value.
Potential P-gp stimulation noted for MF-8B (C73) is not quantified as an efflux ratio and does not establish low F.
content.decision_summary: L5 gut-wall/efflux records add mechanistic support for high permeability in structurally related piperazine aryloxypropanolamine analogs and do not provide affirmative evidence of F<20%; combined with L1 gold values of 54–150% for related analogs, prediction remains high with high confidence.
